A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same SODA-based dialect-chatbot research. The original methods and experiments can be matched despite the expanded title and added speech study. The main text, figures, tables, and appendices support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: Sections 4–5 report an original human evaluation of three LLM families at three dialect intensities against an SAE control, involving 12 evaluators and 95 retained dialogues.

after.justification: Section 4 reports original text-chatbot results, an additional spoken-chatbot evaluation with eight evaluators, and feature-tagging accuracy and linguistic-feature analyses.

M1.justification: The original prompted SAE-to-AAVE text transformation is substantially retained. Section 3.2 adds an F5 text-to-speech pipeline conditioned on reference voices, with text normalization, sentence segmentation, audio concatenation, and speaker cues. This introduces a substantive speech-generation component.

E1.justification: The five SODA dialogue domains remain. v2 adds spoken-dialogue evaluation using African American and Standard American voices, with reference audio from the Corpus of Regional African American Language and LibriSpeech. It also introduces a 90-text linguistic-feature identification test set, expanding both modality and task coverage.

E2.justification: The text comparison retains GPT-4o, Claude-Sonnet-3.5, Llama3.1-70B, and the SAE control. The new speech comparison introduces an SAE/Standard American voice baseline and an SAE/African American voice condition alongside dialect variants. Section 4.3 additionally compares GPT-4o and Claude for feature tagging, substantially expanding the comparison design.

E3.justification: v2 adds a five-condition speech evaluation with eight evaluators and speech-specific metrics, plus feature-tagger testing on 90 texts containing 136 labels and analysis of 250 translated responses per chatbot. For text evaluation, v1 reports 95 retained dialogues, including 41 double-rated; v2 describes 100 dialogues with at least half double-rated without reconciling these accounts. Appendix E also explicitly reverses Offensiveness scores.

E4.justification: Section 4.3 and Figure 2 add analysis of phonetic, morphological, syntactic, and semantic changes across models and dialect strengths. Section 7 adds a qualitative consistency check using evaluators who participated in both modalities. Conversely, v1's attitude-stratified analysis in Figure 2 and its accompanying subjectivity discussion are removed.

E5.justification: Both versions report 95% confidence intervals around human-rating means; applying that practice to speech does not introduce a new uncertainty procedure. However, v2 removes v1's reported inter-annotator agreement range of 0.11–0.36, reducing reliability reporting.

E6.justification: v2 adds feature-identification accuracies of 91% for Claude versus 86% for GPT, linguistic-feature distributions, and speech ratings showing benefits from an African American voice on several conversational measures. Existing text means also change between v1 Figure 1 and v2 Figure 3, while attitude-stratified results disappear. The changed sample account prevents interpreting the text updates as established same-setting gains.

T1.justification: The dialect-transformation mapping E(I, Da, Db) to O is retained with equivalent terminology. Neither version supplies theoretical proofs, and v2's linguistic background and TTS descriptions do not introduce new mathematical definitions or derivations.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes AAVE-speaking users' preference for SAE chatbots. v2 retains that finding for text but makes modality dependence central: African American voices can improve spoken-chatbot reception. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion accordingly expand the contributions from dialect generation to dialect-and-voice personalization.

C2.justification: v2 introduces hypotheses connecting poor high-intensity ratings to excessive phonetic rewriting, speech limitations to SAE-oriented TTS training, and SAE preference to historical technological expectations. It also acknowledges partially different evaluator cohorts across modalities. v1's attitude-based interpretation and specific recommendation for optional dialect customization are removed.

D1.justification: Appendix B newly discloses temperature zero, five-beam Llama decoding, F5 defaults, exact source-audio identifiers, and stated release of reference clips. Sections 3.2 and 4.4 document audio processing and participant eligibility, while Appendix D supplies tagging examples and a prompt. The text-generation settings are newly documented, not established changes to the earlier procedure.

R1.justification: Related work gains substantial AAE linguistic background and a dedicated accented-speech discussion, including Green, Wolfram, and Pinhanez and colleagues. New speech-generation and linguistic-resource references support positioning the work around dialect features and accent-enabled chatbots evaluated by their intended users.

P1.justification: The abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten, AAVE terminology largely becomes AAE, and the title and author list change. The original Approach and Results and Discussion organization becomes a subdivided chatbot-design section, expanded experiments, and separate discussion. References move before the reorganized appendices.

P2.justification: v2 adds a pipeline diagram, feature-distribution chart, speech-result panels, and speech-evaluation interface. The retained text-results figure uses darker colors, distinct markers, reordered panels, and horizontal SAE reference lines instead of separate baseline points. Prompt, metric, and example tables are relocated or restructured, with the response examples expanded.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens the empirical basis of the conclusions: feature analysis examines what the models actually change, and the speech comparisons show that the negative text findings do not apply uniformly across modalities. The added implementation details also improve reproducibility. Removing attitude-stratified results and agreement statistics, and leaving text-sample changes unexplained, weakens transparency; nevertheless, the gains in measurement and support for a more qualified central conclusion outweigh those losses.
